# KV Cache: A Technical Overview

## What Is KV Cache?

KV cache is an optimization technique used in transformer-based language models to avoid redundant computations during autoregressive generation. In transformers, each token's representation depends on all previous tokens through self-attention mechanisms. During inference, generating token N requires computing attention between token N and all tokens 1 through N−1. Without caching, the model would recompute these attention operations from scratch for every new token, leading to quadratic computational complexity relative to sequence length.

KV cache addresses this inefficiency by storing the computed key and value matrices from previously processed tokens in memory. When generating subsequent tokens, the model retrieves these cached values rather than recalculating them. Only the keys and values for the current token need fresh computation, which can then be appended to the cache for future use.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

As context windows expand toward hundreds of thousands of tokens—a trend driven by techniques like RoPE embeddings, sliding window attention, and sparse attention patterns—the computational burden of attention mechanisms grows substantially. Without KV caching, inference time would scale linearly with context length even when generating just a single token, making interactive applications and real-time responses impractical for extended contexts.

KV caching transforms this scaling behavior. By amortizing the cost of processing historical tokens across all future generations, it enables efficient handling of long documents, multi-turn conversations, and codebases. Modern systems further optimize this through techniques such as paged attention (which manages memory fragmentation), KV quantization (which reduces memory footprint), and speculative decoding (which leverages KV reuse for parallel generation). These advances make it feasible to deploy large language models with context
